canberra.title: ‘Mind blowing’ senior public sector salaries and payouts revealed in Senate Estimates
canberra.snippet: The high earnings of some senior public sector executives have dominated a number of Senate Estimates hearings this week, with revelation...
canberra.content:
Millionaire’s factory: 17 Future Fund employees are earning at least double the PM’s salary. Image: Screenshot.

The high earnings of some senior public sector executives have dominated a number of Senate Estimates hearings this week, with revelations of massive salaries and even payouts and bonuses.

There are now 17 public servants from a single agency, the Future Fund Management Agency, earning more than a million dollars a year, with one being paid $2.2 million (including incentive bonuses) in the last financial year.

There were a mere 11 executives earning more than a million at the Future Fund the previous year, but they’ve now been joined by another six top-earning executives.

The Future Fund’s chief corporate affairs officer, Will Hetherton, justified the payroll bill taxpayers are lumped with by telling an Estimates hearing the fund returned 14.8 per cent in the last financial year and added $37.4 billion to the portfolio.

“The Future Fund is really quite distinct from other agencies and departments within the public service,” he said.

“Our job is to maximise risk-adjusted returns, and we operate in competitive global markets both for investment opportunities and talent. The board’s remuneration strategy reflects that.

“Short-term incentives and long-term incentives are tied directly to investment performance.

“A large part of the remuneration that is paid and reported in detail in annual reports is at risk and reflects the strong performance of the fund.”

Greens senator Barbara Pocock couldn’t believe what she was hearing, and described $2.2 million as an “outrageous sum of money” for a single public servant to earn.

“What’s more, we see the number of highly paid people on more than a million bucks in the Future Fund leaping from 11 to 17, and only one woman among them,” she said.

“Australians across the country, who can barely afford groceries, will share my outrage.”

Senator Pocock later compared such annual incomes to a lottery ticket.

“$2.2 million is equivalent to a lottery win – it is an outrageous sum of money for a single public servant to earn,” she said.

“It’s more than double what the head of the Department of Health and Ageing is paid. Why does this government value finance jobs so much more than massive care responsibilities?

“What kind of public service work warrants a salary of $1 or 2 million dollars? Even the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister don’t earn this much. I think most taxpayers would question whether this represents good value for money.”

Australia Post CEO Paul Graham trousered a $1.2 million bonus. Photo: James Braund (Australia Post).

Another hearing heard that Australia Post’s outgoing chief executive officer, Paul Graham, was paid a $1.2 million bonus on top of his $1.64 million base salary in the last financial year.

The bonus was partly due to the $139.4 million sale of Australia Post property, giving it a fourth year of profit.

Mr Graham will retire in June next year. He told the hearing that a “property strategy we had to execute” that was “critical to Australia Post’s transformation” had helped secure him his bonus.

“We do have the great fortune of sitting on property that has been in the network for some time, and it was important for us to get an articulated, clear strategy,” he said.

“Releasing those non-core properties from our portfolio and ensuring that they provided the cash flow that not only got us back into a profitable position, but enabled us to make the substantial investments we’re making as part of our transformation.”

Liberal senator Sarah Henderson, however, told the retiring CEO that his bonus was a “mind-blowing” amount of money.

Estimates has also learned that sacked Department of Employment and Workplace Relations secretary Natalie James received an $828,980 “termination benefit” after her dismissal in February, 18 months short of her contract.

Meanwhile, the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) told hearings this week that it spent almost $1 million on consultants to address staff payroll issues.

Chief operating officer Sanandan Dasgupta said that as of 31 August, the agency had paid $924,664 to advisory firm KordaMentha and KPMG for payroll reviews, remediations and audits.

He said KPMG identified $1.86 million in potential underpayments and $1.54 million in potential overpayments.

It was subsequently stressed that the figures were estimates.

Independent ACT senator David Pocock asked if the huge consultancy spend had actually sorted out the payroll issues.

NEMA’s interim coordinator-general, Pat Hetherington, confirmed they had not.

“There are still some ongoing, unresolved issues,” Mr Hetherington said.

“It’s very easy to oversimplify what it takes to address a payroll issue of 400 people over multiple years where terms and conditions across each pay could be different.

“I remain comfortable that that expenditure has been value for money.”

canberra.title: Arsonist’s fire condemns apartment complex, $300,000 needed in repairs
canberra.snippet: An arsonist has been sentenced for starting a large fire in his own apartment complex, ultimately resulting in all tenants being evacuate...
canberra.content:
28 October 2026

Alexander Peter Brown was charged with arson before he was granted bail earlier this year. Photo: Albert McKnight.

An arsonist has been sentenced for starting a large fire in his own apartment complex, ultimately resulting in all tenants being evacuated as the entire complex was condemned.

Alexander Peter Brown was granted bail before he eventually pleaded guilty to a charge of arson and was sentenced by the ACT Supreme Court this month.

According to a recently published decision, police were called about a large fire in the basement carpark of an apartment building on De Burgh Street, Lyneham, on 5 December 2025.

Brown lived at this 15-unit complex, which was occupied by Housing ACT tenants.

During the evacuation, a fellow resident spotted him outside and asked whether he started the blaze.

“Yes, I’m sorry. I went downstairs and lit a scooter on fire,” he replied.

The resident punched Brown in the face, breaking his cheekbone and knocking him to the ground. He lay there on his back for some time and later needed surgery for his injury.

After extinguishing the flames, ACT Fire and Rescue and Housing ACT assessed the building and determined the entire complex was unsafe for occupancy because of the fire’s impact.

All tenants were moved out and given emergency accommodation. Since then, some have been rehomed while others remained in temporary accommodation, such as hotels.

“The current weekly cost to Housing ACT to rehome and provide temporary accommodation is estimated to be $4500,” the court decision says.

“As of 11 March 2026, the entire unit complex remains vacant awaiting repairs.”

The repairs were expected to take 12 to 18 months to complete after they began and were estimated to cost at least $300,000. However, this did not include the cost of additional remediation such as elevator or structural repairs.

Acting Justice James Stewart said Brown intended to exact revenge on a fellow resident of his own complex by setting the scooter on fire.

“The fire was lit in the basement carpark of the premises using hand sanitiser and a lighter,” he said.

“This crime has had a deep and long-lasting effect on the victims.

“The tendered photos really do explain the tragedy of modern and bespoke public housing being reduced to a useless monument to the offender’s criminality.”

Brown, now aged 36, was born on the southern coast of NSW, is a qualified chef and struggled with mental health and drugs. He was affected by drugs at the time of the fire.

During his sentencing, he said the arson was “the biggest and worst mistake of my life”.

Acting Justice Stewart accepted that he had taken complete responsibility and found he suffered extra-curial punishment when the fellow resident punched him in the face.

While Brown was granted bail in January, he was then taken into custody the following month and remained there until he was sentenced earlier in October.

He was convicted and sentenced to nearly 10 months’ jail, backdated to account for all his time in custody, so he was released immediately.

canberra.title: Youth care worker accused of grooming, indecently abusing underage boy
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse. A woman has been accused of grooming and indecently abusing an underage boy ...
canberra.content:
The 22-year-old woman was granted bail by the ACT Magistrates Court earlier this month. Photo: Albert McKnight.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse.

A woman has been accused of grooming and indecently abusing an underage boy while she was employed as a youth care worker in Canberra.

The 22-year-old woman, who hasn’t been named for now, was granted bail earlier this month before court documents were obtained outlining the allegations against her.

There are no legal orders preventing her from being identified, but despite being aware that Region was planning to report on her case for several days, ACT Policing made a last-minute request, about 30 minutes before this article had originally been scheduled to be published, that she not be named out of concerns for the boy’s well-being.

Shortly afterwards, the ACT Health and Community Services Directorate sent Region an “urgent” letter warning of potential legal action if her name was reported.

According to court documents, the woman worked as a youth care worker for an organisation in Canberra when she met the boy, who was under 16, through mutual connections.

He allegedly began sending her money so she could buy him vapes earlier in 2026.

It is later alleged that the woman and the boy went to watch a movie at the cinema rated MA15+. She allegedly brought Vodka Smirnoff drinks with her and gave some to him, resulting in him becoming drunk.

After leaving the movie, the boy told her he had romantic feelings towards her. She allegedly suggested she felt the same way.

It is alleged the pair kissed in the woman’s car on another occasion.

Then in June, the woman allegedly snuck the boy into her bedroom, as she lived with her family, then exposed herself to him.

It is alleged she asked him to have sex, but he declined. However, she allegedly indecently touched his body before they went to sleep in her bed.

The following evening, she allegedly texted him.

“Idk why but you tryna make me jealous just made me wanna do all types of things with you and I know I said I wanted to hold off, but it’s too hard [sic] … I’d sneak you in again,” the message allegedly said.

In July 2026, the woman’s employer heard allegations that she had been providing vapes and alcohol to children and she was fired from her job.

The boy then went to police in September and alleged the woman had propositioned him for sex on three occasions.

He also claimed that when she gave him her mobile phone number, she asked him to save it on his phone under an alias.

The woman was arrested the following month. When she was interviewed by police, it is alleged she admitted kissing the boy, buying him vapes, giving him alcohol, sending him the text message and sneaking him into her home.

She was charged with grooming, committing an act of indecency on a person under 16, supplying liquor to a young person and using a carriage service to procure sexual activity with a person under 16.

She faced the ACT Magistrates Court on 17 October and applied for bail, which prosecutors opposed.

However, Magistrate Amy Begley ultimately granted bail on conditions including that she not contact the boy, not work as a support worker, not provide care to anyone under 18 and not be alone in the company of anyone under 18 unless in a public place.

The matter was adjourned to 17 November. It was unclear if pleas had been entered.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: ACT Government given 60 days to reveal public housing records as 588 homes sit vacant
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government has agreed to a 60-day deadline to provide detailed records of public housing vacancies, maintenance and spending afte...
canberra.content:
The ACT Government has agreed to provide detailed public housing records within 60 days following a motion passed by the Legislative Assembly. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

The ACT Government has agreed to a 60-day deadline to provide detailed records of public housing vacancies, maintenance and spending after the Legislative Assembly unanimously backed a Crossbench push for greater transparency.

The agreement comes as 588 public housing properties sit vacant while 3652 approved applicants wait for a home, with standard applicants facing an average wait of more than five years, according to figures cited in the Assembly.

The motion, jointly moved by Greens MLA Rebecca Vassarotti and independent MLA Thomas Emerson, calls for ministerial briefings, maintenance reports, vacancy figures and spending records to be provided to the Assembly.

The government initially faced a proposed 30-day deadline, but members agreed to extend it to 60 days following negotiations with Minister for Housing and Homelessness Suzanne Orr.

Mr Emerson told the Assembly the public housing waiting list had grown by more than 600 households since 2024, while only 71 per cent of existing properties met an acceptable standard, down from 81 per cent in 2016.

He said the figures showed a system struggling to meet demand. “Something is fundamentally broken here,” he said.

“We need to look under the hood and see what’s going on, which is what this motion’s about.”

Ms Vassarotti said the Assembly regularly received government updates describing progress on housing programs, but tenants and community organisations were reporting a different experience. “We hear stories of repairs taking too long. We hear concerns about vacant properties remaining empty while housing waitlists grows,” she said.

She said the motion would help establish whether government spending on repairs and new housing was translating into better conditions for tenants.

The requested documents cover the Growing and Renewing Public Housing Program, the Housing Australia Future Fund, the Social Housing Accelerator, the Public Housing Pipeline Program and repairs and maintenance.

The Assembly will also receive information on vacancy turnaround times, maintenance work orders, spending and performance indicators, along with updates on bringing some maintenance services back into government management.

The Canberra Liberals backed the motion, with Shadow Minister for Social Housing and Homelessness Chiaka Barry accusing the government of failing to maintain properties to acceptable standards.

“The government expects private landlords to have a minimum standard and to stick to it, but they haven’t held themselves to the same standard,” she said.

“They should be the ideal landlord, but they’re not.”

Ms Barry said standard public housing applicants were waiting an average of 1875 days, while standard transfer requests took 1586 days.

She described a constituent whose roof had collapsed and who, she said, had been waiting three months for repairs. Orr said the government had worked constructively with the Crossbench to make the extensive request manageable.

She said some records would need to be redacted to protect tenants’ personal circumstances and the locations of sensitive public housing properties.

The government also warned that some of the requested ongoing reporting would require new systems and data collection.

“This will require us to generate information that we don’t currently necessarily have, to report in that particular way,” Ms Orr said.

She cautioned that there could initially be uncertainty around the validation of some figures as reporting arrangements were developed.

Responding to criticism of the government’s handling of public housing, Ms Orr rejected suggestions that ministers did not care about tenants.

“It’s certainly not my position, and it’s not a sentiment that I have experienced with my colleagues either,” she said.

Ms Vassarotti said the concern was not whether the government cared, but whether that concern was producing results.

“It’s around the need to translate that into real action,” she said.

The amended motion passed the Assembly, requiring the government to provide the requested records and ongoing reports on the performance of the public housing system.

canberra.title: A counter-culture festival, cocktails and (vegan) croissants: Four foodie treats to tempt you this November
canberra.snippet: There’s a couple of events coming up in the city for folks who like food, fun and games. Whether you’re looking for pop-up treats, want t...
canberra.content:
Clubb Chess runs over three Sundays in November. Photo: Supplied.

There’s a couple of events coming up in the city for folks who like food, fun and games. Whether you’re looking for pop-up treats, want to rock out in a laneway, or show off your skills at chess over a cocktail, we’ve got just the thing for you.

Clubb Chess, Such and Such

Clubb Chess is an interactive exhibition of art-meets-games at Such and Such. Over three Sundays in November, the uber-cool wine bar will transform into a mini-games festival. Eight contemporary artists and designers have created or reimagined chess, and other games, with unique boards and sets.

There’s a whole new game from Hands On Studio (inspired by classic card game UNO) and artist April Phillips has made her own version of The Game of Life. Attendees can book a time slot to play the 10 specially designed games across the afternoon, and everyone is encouraged to BYO their favourite games to play outside.

For serious chess players, there will be an opportunity to test their skills during a simul (short for simultaneous exhibition) where one player competes in eight simultaneous games.

Your ticket gives you access to all the games, plus DJ sets in the afternoon and live music in the evening. The first Sunday will feature local rockers The King Hits and Sydney’s Tee Vee Repairmann. The bands will change each week, so folks can come back for a different soundtrack each time.

Pilot’s own Tom Opie will be slinging drinks and soft serve, and Tukka By the Bush will be making Johnny Cakes with native condiments.

The whole thing is a combination of a Sunday session and a board games night, all part of Canberra’s Craft and Design Festival.

Clubb Chess will be held on 15, 22 and 29 November from midday to 8:30 pm. Such and Such is located at 8/220 London Circuit, Canberra. Find out more about Clubb Chess and book ahead, or walk-in on the day.

Squeak Out3 is taking the grassroots festival to a whole new level. Photo: Darcy Oliver – Umami Creations.

Squeak Out3: Tokyo Drift, Verity Lane

Squeaky Clean is celebrating their third annual laneway festival, Squeak Out3: Tokyo Drift. Turning their laneway into a beer garden, this event will celebrate the counter-cultural communities who call Squeaky their local.

The Squeak Out laneway parties are legendary for being raucous and brilliant. There will be a host of local bands playing throughout the day, culminating in sets from Brisbane’s Radium Dolls and Scream Feeder, and Sydney’s Rage Flower. If you like loud music, great drinks and a sweaty mosh pit, then you know where you need to be.

“This event is about celebrating Canberra’s counter cultures and giving back to the whole city,” said Squeaky Clean owner and festival director Jono Murphy.

“We keep it free so everyone can get amongst it, this is a party for everyone.

“It’s really important to celebrate artists and creatives in the place that you live, that’s what gives a city its soul and we believe that creative expression is one of the most fundamental parts of being a human.”

A live art battle will see Sancho’s Dirty Laundry and Red Ink Magazine go head-to-head painting on canvas panels in the laneway throughout the day. The resulting art will be auctioned off with all proceeds going to the Canberra Alliance for Harm Minimisation and Advocacy (CARHMA). Freestyle Tattoo Studio will be hosting a flash day in their studio (including exclusive tattoo designs created for the festival) and Canberra Skate Association will be exhibiting the best of their skaters.

There will food trucks from locals like the Harmonie German Club, as well as plenty of cold drinks from Squeaky Clean.

“The first year of Squeak Out (2023) was super grassroots, and since then some seriously experienced event operators have knocked on our door wanting to contribute.

“The team this year has really taken things to the next level, turning Squeak Out into a heavyweight event that I think is gonna blow some socks off.”

Squeak Out3: Tokyo Drift will take place on 21 November at Verity Lane, Civic, from midday until 11 pm. Follow Squeaky Clean on Instagram for more.

Shake ‘n’ Bake is a one-off collab featuring great food and drinks. Photo: Supplied.

Shake ‘n’ Bake, Dairy Road

This one-day event brings together a gang of Canberra hospo mates for a day in the sun out at Under Bakery’s Dairy Road location. A special bakery menu is in the works for the event – alone worth the trip to Fyshwick – but wait, there’s more.

Drinks on the day will be served by award-winning bartender Brett Nebauer (formerly of 11e Cave, currently at Bar Nova) and Pilot’s own Tom Opie (who wins a prize for two mentions in the same article. He’s a busy guy!)

Spirits are pouring courtesy of Marionette Liqueur: an Australian brand bringing a local, craft sensibility to liqueurs like curaçao, cassis, and fruit-based bevs like apricot brandy and an elderflower liqueur which is just begging to be turned into a spritz. And local legends Barrio will also be serving coffees.

Good food, good mates, and good cocktails: what else do you want?

Shake ‘n’ Bake will be held on 2 November, from 2 pm to 6 pm at 1 Dairy Road, Fyshwick. Follow Under Bakery on Instagram for more details.

Dessert Quartets will be bringing their market-favourite treats to the Food Co-op. Photo: Dessert Quartets.

Dessert Quartets pop-up, Canberra Food Co-op

Local vegan business Dessert Quartets is hosting a pop-up bakery at The Canberra Food Co-op every Sunday until the end of November. Run by 100 per cent vegan baker Teresa McTaggart, the pop-up will feature drinks like a vegan iced raspberry matcha latte with cold foam, and savoury bites like a two cheese toasty and mushroom bagel.

But it’s pastry work where Dessert Quartets really shines. A discipline based so thoroughly on butter and eggs requires a lot of skill to vegan-ify and Teresa has these skills in spades. She’s taken inspiration from the wild flavours of legendary croissant store Lune and put her own twist on them. Twice-baked mocha, finger bun and birthday cake flavoured croissants will take pride of place next to cruffins, danishes and macarons filled with a whisky chocolate ganache.

Dessert Quartets is popping up at The Canberra Food Co-operative, Kingsley Street, Acton, from 11 am to 3 pm (or sold out) every Sunday until 29 November. Follow Dessert Quartets on Instagram to get a sneak peek at the weekly menu.

australia.title: Menindee Lakes water levels drop to lowest in five years as experts warn of mass fish deaths
australia.snippet: NSW government imposes water restrictions after Menindee water volumes fall below 2021 levels Sign up for climate and environment editor ...
australia.content:
Water levels at Menindee Lakes in western New South Wales have fallen to their lowest point in five years, prompting the state government to impose upstream water use restrictions as experts warn of potential mass fish deaths over summer.

Combined storage at Menindee Lakes fell below 480 gigalitres earlier this month, the first time since 2021.

In the upper Menindee Lakes, water volumes have dropped below 250GL, a level that triggers temporary state water restrictions across parts of the northern Murray-Darling basin.

The restrictions limit access for some irrigators and are intended to preserve water for critical human needs and the environment.

It follows periods of low rainfall in the catchment throughout the past 12 months, with experts warning of a growing risk of summer fish kills unless flows down to Menindee Lakes via the Darling-Baaka River improve.

Menindee was the site of catastrophic fish kills in 2018, 2019 and 2023, which saw millions of dead fish wash up along stretches of the Darling-Baaka.

“Government officials are predicting with a level of certainty that unless there’s more water flowing into the Baaka-Darling River that there will be fish kills at Menindee this summer,” said Prof Jamie Pittock of the Australian National University and the Wentworth Group of Concerned Scientists.

“We need a major rainfall event to happen and for the state governments to prevent irrigators from pumping out the first flush of water.”

Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter

Graeme McCrabb, who was one of the first Menindee residents to raise the alarm about the 2018-19 disasters, said the combined Menindee Lakes had reached “drought reserve volumes”.

He said this effectively meant conservation of water “at all costs”. McCrabb said he was hopeful that recent rainfall in Queensland may result in some replenishment of the Menindee system.

“There are some small inflows coming across the Queensland border now which probably give us some hope for the summer. But we would need more on top of that,” he said.

“If we don’t get inflows, the risk [of fish kills] would be very high in January or February.”

He said a milder summer would also lower the risk.

“I’m worried about fish kills to be honest,” McCrabb said.

“It’s a tough time or sad time when the water starts to get that real green algal look.”

Days after winning the 2023 state election, the premier, Chris Minns, and senior state ministers visited Menindee and committed to an investigation of the mass fish kills.

An expert panel was established under the northern basin connectivity program, which recommended limiting upstream overextraction during dry periods, to help maintain flows in tributaries into the Darling-Baaka River to Menindee Lakes. This was to try to reduce the risk of catastrophes such as fish kills and large-scale drying.

The panel delivered its final report two years ago but the state government is yet to implement it.

McCrabb said he was disappointed the government had not followed through on the recommendations of the connectivity panel.

“Since the fish kills, government agencies have made no policy changes to improve water quality outcomes,” he said.

Comment has been sought from the NSW water minister, Rose Jackson.

australia.title: Victoria’s 2026 state election could have ‘great consequences’ for politics across Australia. What do voters need to know?
australia.snippet: Labor is chasing a fourth consecutive term and the Liberals are hoping for a breakthrough – but could One Nation end up with the balance ...
australia.content:
Antony Green has covered elections for decades. But the ABC’s former election analyst says the result of the Victorian election will have “greater consequences for the course of national politics than any state election in my lifetime”.

Labor is chasing an unprecedented fourth consecutive term in Victoria under the premier, Ben Carroll – the party’s third leader in four years.

The Liberals, under Jess Wilson, are hoping to turn years of internal division into an electoral breakthrough but to get there the Coalition need to hold all their seats and pick up 16 more.

Further complicating their pathway to victory is One Nation, which, if polling holds, could end up with the balance of power in the lower house. It means for the first time, Pauline Hanson’s party could have a say on who governs a state – and on what terms.

So, how does it all work and what do voters need to know?

australia.title: Electricity, insurance and eggs: see how has life in Australia got more expensive
australia.snippet: Our inflation explorer tracks how prices have risen – or fallen – since 2022 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast...
australia.content:
It has been nearly five years since inflation crashed on to Australia’s shores, as a rebounding post-Covid economy collided with a world of constrained supply.

The global cost-of-living crisis – or affordability crisis, as the Americans call it – has shaped our world from 2022 onwards.

It was also the year that Russia invaded Ukraine, triggering the first of two global energy shocks.

The second energy shock, of course, arrived this February, when the United States and Israel decided to go to war with Iran.

It’s in no small part due to the ongoing Middle East conflict, and the associated surge in fuel costs, that inflation in Australia jumped to 4.3% in the year to September.

While we remain focused on the dramas of 2026, it’s worth taking a longer-term view on how cost-of-living pressures have accumulated in recent years.

For example, fuel costs have risen by more than 20% in the past year, but over the longer term they have matched overall inflation (which is still a pretty big increase).

Our inflation explorer tracks all the categories included in the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ consumer price index.

Inflation explorer: showing the change in price for various goods and services

Hover or tap on lines to show the item names, or use the dropdowns to highlight different items or groups or switch between the price index and yearly % change in the price. The 'all groups CPI' line shows the change over time for all goods and services combined - this is the so-called 'basket' of goods and services. Data has been re-indexed to 100 at the 2021 December quarter

Highlight:

Data type:

Guardian graphic. Data source: ABS

Our interactive chart shows inflation has climbed 23% since the end of 2021.

But which goods and services have soared by more than that over recent years, and which haven’t?

You can explore the data at your own pace, but here are some highlights.

Bills, bills, bills

No surprise that electricity is among the costs that have increased the most. Household power bills are up by 35% since the start of 2022.

The chart shows the zigzagging line as federal and state government subsidies have turned on and off. It’s clear also that these subsidies, while welcome at the time, did nothing to change the upwards trend. Relatedly, gas is also up 49%.

Another cost that is hard to avoid is insurance, and the chart shows premiums have surged by 46% in nearly five years. Rental costs are 27% higher. Homebuilding costs are 36% higher.

Postal services are up 40%. Speaking of essentials, supermarket staples like oil and eggs have increased by more than 40%, and bread, milk and fruit prices are up more than 30% in five years.

On the upside, chicken and vegetables have increased by less than inflation.

Not all bad news

The chart shows that, generally, the lowest price increases over recent years are for non-essentials.

Household items like glassware, tableware and household utensils are actually cheaper. Electrical items, toasters and so forth, are on average no more expensive now than they were at the end of 2021.

Women’s clothing is just 7% more expensive, and men’s only 4%.

The biggest price decline has been in public transport fees – down 5%, presumably thanks to state and territory government decisions.

Perhaps the most surprising result is that childcare costs, while they have been rising of late, are only up 7% since the end of 2021.

australia.title: Alastair Campbell on Trump, political violence and why populist politics doesn’t work - podcast
australia.snippet: It’s election season: the US midterms are just days away and Israel, Brazil and Serbia have all had consequential elections this week. Al...
australia.content:
It’s election season: the US midterms are just days away and Israel, Brazil and Serbia have all had consequential elections this week. Alastair Campbell from The Rest is Politics podcast co-host speaks with political editor Tom McIlroy about our ‘high-octane political environment’ and why he argues that populist politics began in the aftermath of the global financial crisis.

Following last week’s alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines, Campbell also reflects on how the UK responded to violence towards its own politicians – including Jo Cox, David Amess and Ann Widdecombe.

The former journalist and staffer to Tony Blair has just released his 22nd book Persevilience: The Word the World Needs Now, and will be touring Australia next month

australia.title: Australia must recruit hundreds more to crew Aukus submarines, retired admiral warns
australia.snippet: As USS Colorado showcases the program in Perth, Peter Briggs says personnel is just one of the ‘huge issues’ it faces Get our breaking ne...
australia.content:
Australia faces an uphill battle to recruit and train enough naval personnel to serve on submarines planned for the future fleet of nuclear-powered vessels under the controversial $368bn Aukus deal, a retired admiral has warned.

As the Virginia-class submarine USS Colorado arrived at HMAS Stirling south of Perth on Tuesday for a month of routine maintenance and to help build Australian expertise, retired admiral Peter Briggs said more people needed to be enrolled in the navy’s submarine program.

As part of a $368bn trilateral defence deal, Australia will acquire between three and five Virginia-class, nuclear-powered submarines from the United States to replace its five diesel-electric Collins-class vessels, which are becoming obsolete.

The new submarines are much bigger and require up to 134 crew – almost three times the number needed for the Collins class.

The Royal Australian Navy says it has 230 personnel in various stage of the US nuclear-powered submarine training pipeline.

“Of these, approximately 145 have completed US Naval nuclear power training and are now building experience training on US Navy SSNs [a hull classification for nuclear-powered submarines],” a navy spokesperson said.

“By 2030, we expect to have 400 Royal Australian Navy officers and sailors trained and ready to serve.”

But Briggs urged a more intensive recruitment plan to crew the bigger boats.

“We have got to triple the size of the submarine arm and we’ve got to train them in nuclear skills,” he said.

“You are heading toward needing a submarine arm of 3,000, that’s the hill you have to climb.”

Approximately 850 submariners are qualified to operate Collins-class vessels.

The Virginia-class boats are intended to bridge the transition from the Collins-class fleet to the future SSN-AUKUS submarine, an even bigger design being developed by Australia and the UK.

“The personnel side is a huge issue, but it’s not the only one,” Briggs said.

The former submariner argued that maintaining two different submarine types would add complexity to training, logistics, maintenance and spare-parts arrangements.

The Australian government did not respond to questions about recruitment targets and whether a workforce development program was on track.

Recruitment is further complicated by the need for more than a dozen different trades, from radio and sonar operators to cooks and electricians.

After spending the next month is Perth, the USS Colorado will return to the city’s waters again in late 2027 as part of the Submarine Rotational Force-West program which is designed to help Australia build the skills and infrastructure to operate its own nuclear fleet.

From 2027, the program will see up to four US and one UK nuclear-powered submarine rotate through HMAS Stirling.

Paul Johnson, HMAS Stirling fleet base west commodore, said the USS Colorado maintenance period would be used to “practise and test our procedures across a range of nuclear-related operational scenarios”.

Officials stressed that no radiological material would be transferred during the maintenance period and that nuclear-related exercises would be simulated.

Late last year, Senate estimates heard that US submarines carrying nuclear weapons could rotate through Australian ports despite a non-proliferation commitment.

USS Colorado captain, Justin Reeves, said the US government would not “confirm or deny the presence of nuclear weapons on specific platforms”.

Colorado was built in 2018 and arrived this week carrying conventional weapons, including four torpedoes and four “payload tubes” that can be used to house and launch weapons.

It took two weeks to travel to Perth from Pearl Harbor in Hawaii with 160 men and no women aboard. A sign labelled “Berth Rules”, taped to the wall near the submarine’s entryway, listed “Don’t be stinky” as the crew’s top priority once they reach port.

The demands of living and working in confined spaces for extended periods presents another recruitment challenge for officials.

Sleeping arrangements can involve bunks stacked three high, while “hot racking” allows three sailors to share two beds by rotating their sleeping schedules around watch duties.

In some circumstances, and when accommodation is limited, sailors may sleep in torpedo rooms.

Reeves said the vessel is “built for combat, not for comfort”.

Nuclear submarines don’t need to refuel, meaning their range is effectively infinite. “The limits of its endurance are really food and toilet paper, and that’s several months’ worth,” Reeves said.

“Being nuclear powered is a massive advantage.”

world.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
world.snippet: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah,...
world.content:
Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.

According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.

Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.

Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.

Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

world.title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
world.snippet: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and pos...
world.content:
The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.

“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.

“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.

“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.

Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”

This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.

On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.

France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.

The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.

Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.

The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.

Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.

“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.

At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”

Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.

“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”

world.title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
world.snippet: Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected t...
world.content:
Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.

A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.

The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.

During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.

The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.

Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.

Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.

A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.

A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”

During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.

The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

world.title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño
world.snippet: Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river wh...
world.content:
The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.

“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”

Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.

“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”

Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.

The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.

The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.

Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.

“The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.

Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.

“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.

When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.

Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”

US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”

Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.

Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”

Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.

“In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old.

US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.

Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.

Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.

His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.

Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.

The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.

Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.

“They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.

Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.

Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.

Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.

Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”

Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.

“It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.”

Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.

Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes.

Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region.

Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.

David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”

The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”

Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.

Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.

Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.

Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”

In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.

Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.

El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine.

Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.

Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.

For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.

“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.

Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.

world.title: Sudan paramilitary drone strikes cause mass power cuts in eastern states
world.snippet: Rapid Support Forces strike five power stations in three states controlled by Sudanese army Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces hav...
world.content:
Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country’s east, a government official said.

The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref and one in White Nile state, “resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states”, the official said on condition of anonymity.

All three states are controlled by the Sudanese army, which has been at war with the RSF, its former ally, since April 2023.

The United Nations has repeatedly warned that regular attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people who are already facing the world’s largest hunger crisis.

Babiker Youssef, a resident of Al-Fao, in Gedaref, said the power had been out there since early morning.

“My son is diabetic, his insulin has to be stored in the fridge,” he said over the phone, adding that he feared he would not be able to replace the medication if it spoiled. “We have no idea when the power will come back,” he said.

Electricity has been cut for days at a time after past paramilitary drone strikes on power stations and hydroelectric dams.

Sudan’s war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.

In the first three weeks of October, drone strikes killed more than 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a UN tally.

Africa’s third largest country, home to an estimated 50 million people, has been ravaged by the war, which aid workers estimate has killed more than 200,000 people.

The majority of Sudan’s hospitals have been forced to close, at least 8 million children are out of school and swathes of the country cannot access basic services.

Abdelhafez Daafallah, a 54-year-old farmer, said by phone from Al-Junaid town in Al-Jazira: “The electricity had just started to improve three months ago, the power station the militia had destroyed was just repaired and we had hope our irrigation pumps would finally start running again.

“We hoped we would be able to finally get back to farming, but now the station has been hit,” he said, frustrated after nearly four years unable to work his land.

Farmers in Al-Jazira have struggled to rehabilitate and replant their land since the army recaptured the state from the RSF last year.

To the east, in Gedaref, Ibrahim Mohammed, 37, a grocer, said he was “already facing power cuts for hours before the strike”. “Now I have chicken in the fridge, we either lose our entire stock, or will be forced to sell it off at any price, which is still a loss,” he said.

Sudan is also grappling with unprecedented inflation and its currency has lost more than 25% of its value in recent weeks.
